pb_sidebar.item_run_payroll
A four-step wizard that takes one division and one period and computes a draft payslip for every eligible employee.
It is where a month of salaries starts. Everything downstream — review, approval, the bank file — reads what this step produced, so an error here is an error in all of it.
Once the month's attendance and overtime have been imported and committed. Not before: computing on an uncommitted import is the single most common first-week mistake.
The Payroll Officer group, a committed import for the period, and a formula configuration on the division you are running.
Computing before the month's import is committed. The eligible count is the tell — 12 where you expected 48 means the data is not in yet.
Running the wrong cycle. Mid-cycle pays an advance; end-cycle settles the month. They are not two views of one thing.
Submitting for approval without opening the flagged payslips. A flag is a question the engine wants answered, and submitting is you answering it with silence.

lesson
pb_sidebar.item_pay_runs
runpayroll
A board of every pay run, grouped by the approval stage it is waiting at, with the actions that stage allows on each card.

Nothing is paid without the right sign-offs, and the board is what makes the pipeline visible and auditable. It answers the only question a payroll week really asks: what is stuck, and whose gate is it stuck at.
Daily during payroll week, and any time you need to know where a period has got to.
A computed run. Approving needs the group that owns that particular gate.
Approving a run without opening its flagged payslips. The board shows totals; the flags are on the slips.

Rejecting without a written reason. The product refuses an empty one, and a thin one is worse than none: the run is cancelled either way, and the person who has to rebuild it is guessing at what you saw.
Reading a status column as a period. The columns are approval stages — July and June can sit in the same one.

pb_sidebar.item_payslips
runpayroll
The review surface for individual payslips inside one run: a filterable list, and for the selected employee the approval stepper and the full salary breakdown.
A run total can be right while an individual slip is wrong. This is the only screen that shows the working behind a net figure, so it is where an error is caught before money moves.
After computing and before submitting for approval, and again whenever an employee asks why their pay is what it is.
A computed run to read. No special group is needed to look.
Editing a net amount directly instead of fixing the input and recomputing. The slip then no longer agrees with the data behind it, and the next recompute silently undoes the fix.
Expecting insurance to move when overtime does. BHXH, BHYT and BHTN are charged on the registered base, which overtime does not change.
Clearing a flag by dismissing it. Clearing one means understanding it — the flag was the engine asking a question about that employee.

pb_sidebar.item_import
A guided four-step flow — source, review and match, validate and fix, commit — plus the batch history of everything imported before.
Most wrong payslips start as a wrong row in a file. Fixing it here costs minutes; fixing it after approval costs a retro line and a conversation.
Whenever the month's inputs arrive, and always before computing a run.
The Import group, a file or a connected system to read from, and a formula configuration to map the columns onto.
Committing a batch with unresolved rows because the deadline is close. An unmatched row is an employee who will be missing from the run.
Importing one month's data into another month's period. The batch is named for the period it targets — read that name before committing.
Fixing an import mistake on the payslips afterwards. That corrects the output and leaves the input wrong, so the next recompute brings the mistake back.

pb_sidebar.item_full_final
payruns
The settlement workspace for departing employees, listing what each is still owed and whether it has been paid.
Leaver settlements have legal deadlines and one chance to be right. They are also the payment most likely to be disputed, because it is the last one.
As soon as a resignation or termination date is confirmed — not on the payroll run date, which is usually too late.
A recorded contract end date and a current leave balance for the employee.
Leaving the departing employee in the normal monthly run as well. They are then paid twice, and recovering an overpayment from someone who has left is a legal problem, not a payroll one.
Settling before the last month's attendance is in. The final salary is a prorated month, so it needs the same inputs every other month needs.

payrun
payroll
See exactly how a part-month salary was prorated — day by day, no black box.
calculator
outline
pb_sidebar.item_proration
payslips
An audit trail of every prorated amount in a run — joiners, leavers and unpaid leave — showing days worked, standard days and the factor between them.
Proration is the question employees ask most often, and the one hardest to answer from memory. This screen is the evidence, written down before anyone asks.
When a payslip looks too small and you need to show why, and as a spot check on any run with mid-month movement.
A computed run containing at least one joiner, leaver or unpaid-leave case.
Assuming calendar days when the division's configuration uses standard working days. Twenty-two is not thirty, and the difference is somebody's salary.
Reading the money before the factor. If the factor is right and the amount still looks wrong, the problem is upstream in the contract or the import.

Backdated raises and corrections, applied cleanly to a later run — with a full trail.

outline
pb_sidebar.item_retro
payruns
A ledger of differences owed from periods that are already closed, paid in the current run with the source period recorded on every line.
It keeps closed months closed. Reopening an approved run to fix the past invalidates everything that was reported from it — the retro line is how you pay the difference without doing that.
Backdated raises, allowances missed in an earlier month, and any correction found after the run it belongs to was approved.
The source run is done, and the correction is documented — a retro line without a reason is an unexplained payment.
Editing the old approved payslip instead of creating a retro line. The old month has already been reported; changing it changes a number somebody else has filed.
Leaving the source period blank. Without it the line is money paid for no stated reason, which is exactly what an audit asks about first.

The visible rulebook: every payslip line is a named component with a formula you can read.
calculator
lesson
pb_sidebar.item_formula
A studio for each division's formula configuration — the components, the formula behind each one, what it depends on, and a live preview against a real employee.
It is the answer to every "why is my pay this number" question, written down. A payroll desk that can read the configuration stops guessing and starts showing.
When an allowance is added, when a rule changes, and any time a number on a payslip has to be traced back to where it came from.
The Payroll Officer group to read it and a manager tier to change it, plus a sample employee to preview against.
Editing a live configuration without previewing. The preview costs seconds; a wrong component costs every future payslip in that division.
Renaming a component other formulas depend on. The dependency panel names them — read it before you rename, because a formula that lost its input does not always fail loudly.
Building a statutory rate into a formula by hand. Rates belong on the statutory policy; a hard-typed 8% is one that nobody will remember to change.

Salary Structures
setup
payroll
The legacy rule sets — kept because old payslips still reference them, not because new pay logic belongs here.
layers
outline
pb_sidebar.item_structures
formula
Odoo salary structures and their rules: the older way of computing a payslip, still holding the logic that historical payslips were produced by.
You will meet them the first time you open a payslip from before the migration, and knowing what they are is the difference between reading history and doubting it.
When reading an old payslip, and when migrating a division onto a formula configuration — the structure is what you are migrating FROM.
A manager tier, and the Formula Engine basics — otherwise it is hard to see what the two are for.
Building new pay logic here because it is familiar. A new rule added to a structure is invisible to the Formula Engine, so the division it was meant for never sees it.
Deleting a structure that has no employees on it today. Payslips from three years ago still point at it, and a report run over those months needs it to still be there.

setup
payroll
BHXH · BHYT · BHTN rates, the ceilings, and the thuế TNCN table — the rules the law writes for you.
shield-check
lesson
pb_sidebar.item_statutory
The company's active insurance policy and tax table: who pays what, on which base, up to which ceiling, and from which date.

This is what the company DECLARES it contributes, and it is what the cockpit, the contribution analytics and the statutory reports read. It is not what prices a payslip — that is a parameter in each division's formula configuration — so the real work here is keeping the two in agreement. When they disagree, payroll is running on a rate the company is not declaring.
When a decree changes a rate or a deduction, at the start of a tax year, and whenever an employee asks why a contribution is the amount it is.
A manager tier, and the decree or circular in front of you — this screen records a decision that was made elsewhere.

Editing the rate on the policy that is currently in force. There is no version history to fall back on — the old declared rate is simply gone, and with it the evidence of what the company was declaring last month.

Creating the new policy but dating it from today rather than from the day the decree applies. The effective date is the company's record of when the change legally started, and a date nobody can point at a decree for is the first thing an inspection asks about.

Declaring the new rate and stopping there. The number that prices a payslip is a parameter on the division's formula configuration, so until that is changed too the run still charges the old rate — correctly, and against a declaration that now says otherwise.

outline
pb_sidebar.item_integrations
Configured links to the systems payroll data arrives from — an HR system, a time clock, the bank — with their field mappings and when each last synced.

Data that arrives by itself is data nobody retyped, and most wrong payslips start as a retyped row. The sync history is the part that matters: a connector that stopped looks exactly like one that is working.
Once at onboarding, again whenever a source system changes its fields — and as a two-minute check at the start of every payroll week.
The Integration user group and credentials for the source system.
Leaving a failed sync unnoticed until payroll week. The staged-record count is the tell — rows sitting in staging are a month of attendance that never became inputs.
Assuming a connector that is "connected" is also up to date. Connected describes the credentials; the last-sync time describes the data.

Where you land, what the month looks like, and where everything else lives.
grid
lesson
pb_sidebar.item_dashboard
The command centre: who you are, which run is live, four numbers that describe the company, and a card for each part of the product worth opening today.

It is the only screen that answers "what is the state of payroll right now" without you choosing a filter first. The tiles report it; the buttons and the run rows beside them are the doors into the screens those figures came from.
First thing, every day of payroll week, and any time you have been away long enough to have lost the thread.
Nothing. This is the one screen everybody can open, and it is deliberately the least gated in the product.
Reading a dashboard figure as today's work. Headcount and monthly payroll describe the company; only "pending approval" is a queue, and only one of those is yours.

Treating it as a report and copying the numbers out. The KPI tiles only REPORT — it is the buttons and the run rows that open the screen a figure came from, and a figure copied away from its working loses the part somebody will ask about.
Waiting for the dashboard to tell you something is wrong. It shows what is happening, not what has been checked — a flagged payslip is a number here and a question on the Payslips screen.
approvals
Approvals
overview
payroll
Every run waiting for a signature, in the lane of the gate it is waiting at — including yours.
clipboard-check
lesson
pb_sidebar.item_approvals
dashboard
Three lanes — Officer review, {{hrTierName}}, {{gmTierName}} — with a card per submitted run, the net at stake across all of them, and a list of what has already been decided.

The Pay Runs board shows every run there is; this screen shows only the ones a human still has to answer for. It is the queue, and the number in its header is the part of that queue that will not move until you move it.
Every morning of payroll week, and before you tell anybody a run is stuck — the lane it is in names who is holding it.
One of the payroll approval groups. Without one the leaf is not in your sidebar at all, which is the honest form of "you cannot approve".
Approving from the lane without opening the run. The card shows a total and a payslip count; the flags are on the payslips, and the total is what a wrong payslip hides inside.
Reading an empty lane as a broken screen. Two of the three lanes are empty on most days — that is what a month looks like when nothing is stuck.

Rejecting instead of asking. A rejection CANCELS the whole batch and is recorded with your name on it, and only the {{gmTierName}} tier can reopen it as a draft; a question in the corridor costs nobody two days.

Employees
people
payroll
Everyone payroll can pay — with the two facts that decide whether they will actually be paid.
users
outline
pb_sidebar.item_employees
The people roster: headcount, running contracts, contracts expiring within thirty days, new hires, the monthly wage bill, and a payroll-ready mark on each person.
Payroll-ready is the whole point of this screen. Somebody with no bank account computes perfectly and is not paid, and you find that out either here, in a minute, or on {{payDay}}, from them.
Before a run rather than after it, and whenever somebody joins, leaves or changes department.
The Payroll Officer group or above — the leaf is gated, because a wage list is not something everybody in a company should be able to read.
Reading the wage column as take-home pay. It is the registered contract base — the figure insurance is charged on — and nobody is paid exactly that in any month with overtime in it.
Fixing a person's pay here. This screen holds who they are and what they were hired on; what they were paid last month is a payslip, and the two are corrected in different places.
Using bulk mode without reading the count. It is the one control here that changes many records at once, and "12 selected" is the only thing standing between a helpful edit and twelve wrong ones.

Contracts
people
payroll
The agreements payroll is actually paid from — and the expiry dates that quietly end them.
file-text
outline
pb_sidebar.item_contracts
employees
Every contract with its type, its period and its wage: running, expiring within thirty days, draft and expired, plus the wage bill and the average wage across them.

A person is not a contract. Payroll computes from the contract, so a contract still in draft pays nothing however complete the employee record is — and a contract that expired mid-month is a proration nobody asked for.
In the week before a run, on the expiring filter, and whenever somebody is promoted, transferred or renewed.
The Payroll Officer group or above, and the signed paperwork — this screen records an agreement that was made somewhere else.
Leaving a renewal in draft over the run date. The employee is on the roster, their contract is not running, and the run simply computes without them.
Editing a running contract's wage to correct one month. That changes the insurance base going forward and corrects nothing that has already been paid — the past is a retro line.

Insights
insights
payroll
The board that answers the questions a payroll month asks every time.
trending-up
outline
pb_sidebar.item_analytics

Executive analytics over the runs this company has: the headline net for the LATEST run whatever state it is in, the cost story over three, six or twelve months, a department leaderboard read from the latest DONE run, the statutory split, a workforce pulse and the analytics snapshots panel.

It answers the questions a payroll month asks every time, fast, because it reads the STORED per-run roll-ups rather than re-adding payslip lines. That is also the thing to know about it: the hero and the leaderboard do not have the same scope — the hero shows the latest run and prints its state beside itself, and the leaderboard waits for a run to be done. Read the state chip before you quote the number.
After a run reaches done, at month end, and any time somebody senior asks a question that starts with "why is payroll".
An analytics group, and at least two completed runs — a trend needs a second point before it is a trend.
Comparing a total against a total. Headcount moves between months, so the honest comparison is cost per head — one more employee explains most of what looks like a rise.
Reading a board figure without its window. Three months and twelve months tell different stories about the same company, and the chip that decides which is easy to leave where somebody else left it.

Quoting the headline without its state chip. The hero is the LATEST run in any state — a draft that nobody has reviewed appears here the moment it is computed, and it reads exactly like a paid month unless you look at the chip beside it.
explorer
Explorer
insights
payroll
For the question the board did not anticipate: pick a measure, break it down, filter it.
compass
outline
pb_sidebar.item_explorer
insights
A question builder over the same payroll facts: one measure, one breakdown, one comparison, and any number of filters shown as removable tags above the result.

Boards answer anticipated questions and real ones are rarely anticipated. This is where "net pay by division for the divisions that ran mid-cycle" gets answered without anybody exporting a spreadsheet — and it reconciles with the payslips, which a spreadsheet stops doing the moment it is saved. It is also the only analytics screen that explains a MOVEMENT: a variance waterfall between two periods that adds up exactly, and a drill from any cell down to the employees behind it.
When the board has answered everything it can and the question is still open, and when somebody needs a figure broken down a way nobody built a screen for.
An analytics group and a computed run. Knowing which measure you actually want helps more than any filter.

Quoting a figure without its filters. The tags above the result are part of the answer — the same measure with one tag removed is a different number and looks identical when it is pasted into an email.
Stopping at the table. The waterfall and the drill are where the answer usually is — the table tells you a division moved, and those two tell you which component moved and which employees carried it.

Workforce Analytics
insights
payroll
The same months read as people rather than as money: who was paid, who joined, who left.
bar-chart
outline
pb_sidebar.item_workforce_insights
insights
Headcount paid month by month, joiners and leavers, cost per head, attendance exceptions and overtime — all read off the payroll that was actually run.

"Employees paid" is not "employees employed", and the gap between them is where a missing payslip lives. A month where headcount is flat and cost per head jumps is a different problem from one where both move.
At month end beside Insights, and whenever a run's headcount does not match what you expected.
An analytics group, and at least two runs to compare.
Reading the headcount line as a hiring chart. It counts people who were PAID, so a step in it can equally be a run that left somebody out.
Taking attendance exceptions as somebody else's problem. Each one becomes an input, and the ones nobody resolved are the flags on next month's payslips.
govreports
Government Reports
compliance
payroll
The statutory filings for this company's country, one month at a time.
file-text
outline
pb_sidebar.item_govt_reports
A front door over the filing wizards: the report tiles this company's country has, grouped by the authority that asks for them, prefilled with the company and the month you chose.
Filings have deadlines set by law rather than by the company, and they are read by somebody outside it. This screen is where you find out which ones apply to you without asking who knows.
After the month's runs are done and before the authority's deadline — a filing built on an unfinished month is a filing that will have to be corrected.
Completed runs for the month, and the country's own paperwork rules — Payobook prepares the file, it does not submit it for you.
Generating from a month whose runs are not all done. The tiles read what has been computed, so an unfinished run is a filing that is short by however many payslips are still in the pipeline.

Reading "coming soon" as "Payobook does not do this country". It means the country's own payroll module is not INSTALLED on this database — Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, Cambodia and Malaysia all have filings in the catalogue, and each one appears the moment the module that owns its wizard is there. It is an install question, and the answer is a conversation with whoever administers the system.
